title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:1–17)
hookLine: Paul introduces himself to a church he's never met, and to the good news as power

cards: A letter to strangers is hard to write. You want them to know who you are, and to like you, but you also have something important to say. How do you start?
Paul faces exactly that, writing to the Christians in Rome. He's never been there. He didn't found that church.

He's heard about them, and they've heard about him, perhaps not all of it good. And this letter would go on to turn lives around: Augustine, Luther and Wesley each wrote about the part it played for them.
A new part of the path begins here: Romans. Its first big claim is today's word.

teach.b: Paul opens by telling them who he is: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God." Servant: the Greek word is doulos, a slave, someone who belongs to another.

teach.h: TO ALL IN ROME, CALLED TO BE SAINTS.
teach.b: Then a warm greeting: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace." Saints, as on day three hundred seven: ordinary people, set apart.
He says he longs to visit, so he can give them some spiritual gift.

teach.h: SO WE CAN ENCOURAGE EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Then he catches himself and adds, in effect: I mean, so we can encourage each other. "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me."
The great apostle, correcting himself mid-sentence so he won't sound like he's come to lecture.

Then comes the line the whole letter stands on: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek."

teach.h: FOR I AM NOT ASHAMED OF THE GOSPEL OF CHRIST.
teach.b: Why would anyone be ashamed? Because in Rome, a crucified man was the lowest thing imaginable. The cross was the empire's punishment for slaves and rebels.
And Paul says: I'm not ashamed of it. It's power. The Greek word is dynamis, where we get dynamic.
Then one more line, quoted from the prophet Habakkuk, the line Luther later said set him free: "The just shall live by faith."

how: Christians read Romans in church and in Bible studies, and some memorize Romans 1:16, "I am not ashamed of the gospel," as a statement of confidence in their faith.

too proud ever to admit a fault or failing

games.q: you're Paul, writing to a church in Rome you've never met. you've just said you want to give them some spiritual gift. how do you go on?
o: tell them how much they need your teaching.
correct yourself: so we can encourage each other, both of us.
games.why: he corrects himself: "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me."

practice: Think of someone you don't know yet, a new neighbor, a new coworker, the person you always see and never speak to, and picture yourself saying hello.
Try Paul's way: say who you are, simply; greet them warmly; and let it be mutual, two people encouraging each other, not one giving and one receiving.
If you pray, pray for that person by name, or by face; if you don't, just picture the hello, and let it be warm.

wordCard.voice: Not ashamed. Paul's first big claim in Romans: he's not ashamed of the good news of a crucified Christ, because it is the power of God.

orig.note: Greek: power, ability. Paul's word in Romans 1:16; the root of dynamic.

carryVoice: Your line: someone who belongs to another. That's how Paul introduces himself. Day three hundred twelve, done.
